title: Students’ Acquisition of Science Process Skills in Chemistry through Computer Simulations and Animations in Secondary Schools in Tanzania
venue: International Journal of Learning, Teaching and Educational Research
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether computer simulations and animations improve secondary school students’ acquisition of integrated science process skills in chemistry compared with conventional instructional materials. The problem addressed is the persistent weakness in science process skills in Tanzanian secondary schools, attributed to teacher-centered instruction, limited laboratory resources, and low access to ICT-supported inquiry learning.

The study used a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest comparison with mixed methods. Four public secondary schools in the Dodoma and Singida regions of Tanzania participated, involving 320 level-three chemistry students and 20 chemistry teachers. The treatment group learned chemical kinetics, equilibrium, and energetics using computer simulations and animations (from Yenka Chemistry and PhET), while the control group used conventional materials such as textbooks, diagrams, pictures, models, and laboratory materials. Both groups were taught through a 5E inquiry-based approach, and student focus group discussions provided qualitative data.

Results showed no significant pretest differences between groups, but the treatment group outperformed the control group on the posttest science process skills measure. The authors conclude that computer simulations and animations support students’ inquiry, help them visualize abstract chemistry concepts, and improve skills such as hypothesizing, identifying variables, planning experiments, interpreting data, and drawing conclusions. They recommend wider use of simulations and animations in Tanzanian secondary school chemistry.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental pre/post study with control and treatment groups, plus qualitative triangulation. It is not randomized, but it does provide a reasonably designed comparison with baseline equivalence and clear outcome measures.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports a sizable positive post-test difference on science process skills, with treatment-group gains well above control performance. Because the outcome is a priority K-12 science reasoning skill and the difference is substantial, the impact is best rated green rather than yellow.

interventions.use_case: computer simulations and animations used in secondary school chemistry lessons on chemical kinetics, equilibrium, and energetics to support inquiry-based science process skill development

finding.finding_summary: Students exposed to computer simulations and animations scored substantially higher on the integrated science process skills test than those taught with conventional materials. Post-test means were 65.79 (SD=13.45) for the treatment group versus 48.03 (SD=11.72) for the control group, with a statistically significant between-group difference (p=0.000).
finding.measure: 25-item integrated science process skills test covering hypothesis formation, identifying variables, operationally defining, planning experiments, interpreting data, and drawing conclusions
finding.std_deviation: treatment post-test SD=13.45; control post-test SD=11.72
